newsitem.title: UK: Softs outlook - Coffee may shy away from highs.
newsitem.headline: Softs outlook - Coffee may shy away from highs.

text.p: Coffee futures may stay shy of their recent peaks this week as the market is running into a tentative top, but conditions could remain choppy, trader said.
London's robusta market see-sawed from last Wednesday's nine-month high of $1,820 a tonne to end the week at $1,729.
While more losses could be on the cards as the market corrected down after the explosive rally since the start of 1997, medium- to longer-term prospects remained positive, traders said.
Cocoa could extend last week's rally, which was seen as technically-driven while white sugar was turning bearish on account of last week's series of strong closes.
London coffee futures continued to ride on the back of a volatile New York arabica market, driven by nervous roaster price fixing and origin selling.
New York's May futures breached the psychological $2.00 barrier last week for the first time since the Brazilian frost in June 1994.
The market's underlying strength reflected tight nearby supplies, with both Colombia and Brazil expected to draw on old stockpiles to satisfy strong roaster demand.
London's fortunes also hinged on further roaster buying or fund selling.
"The roasters are slightly short rather than long," said one. But origins sellers, used to seeing higher levels, are unlikely to aggressively follow the market down.
The main factor would be fund long liquidation, and the selling could come in if the slide triggered major sell-stops. Technically, London's May was seen supported by $1,600 in the short term.
Cocoa may sparkle on a fresh wave of short-covering activity. The key May contract rose to a high of 949 stg a tonne on Friday, the highest since December 12.
Technically the rally should continue after consolidation towards 972, but some analysts said changes in the fundamental picture might be needed to justify further price increases.
Attention was focused on the potential for the Ivorian mid crop and weather reports after unusual dryness in February.
Manufacturers remained reluctant to ride on the rally, which had so far totalled 84 stg in two weeks.

This week's cocoa talks among major producer and consumer nations in London were not expected to yield any market-moving news. But they could stir market sentiment if major producers led by Ivory Coast provided crop updates.
In white sugar, traders said the outlook for London's spot May value was turning bearish on account of last week's series of strong closes.
But fundamental news was still thin on the ground, despite increased offtake in the Middle East for raw and white sugar.
"People have turned their thoughts around to the upside...it keeps trying the downside and keeps rallying," said one trader.

Last week May was content to hover in tight ranges, holding above a six-week upward trendline and supported by a cluster of short-term moving averages. But it was still fighting shy of last month's peak of $312.50.
"We're still in this range...and we're not showing anything new technically," the trader said.
London traders said sentiment in whites was most likely to come from the raws market, where speculators and trade players were holding each other at bay and reducing nearby values to a tight range.
